To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) special education teachers are more highly educated than the general teaching population; (2) the majority of special education teachers are female; (3) special education teachers earn more than the average teacher; (4) special education teachers tend to be older than the average teacher and to have more teaching experience than the average teacher.

special education is perceived by teachers and non- teachers alike as a high prestige occupation, that special class teaching is perceived as a higher prestige occupation than regular class teaching, and that there is a high degree of consensus about the relative prestige of the special education occupations.
special education teaching is perceived to have high occupational prestige and is considered to be a highly prestigious teaching area.
In summary, our research is concerned with

three questions: What is the occupational prestige of the special education areas as a whole? How do the special education fields compare with other occupations? How do the fields compare with each other?

the following questions: (1) What are the occupational aspirations of students enrolled in special education programs? (2) What is the occupational standing of special education teachers? (3) What are the attitudes of special education teachers toward the special education areas as occupations?

the following questions: 1. What are the perceptions of the occupational prestige of the special education areas? 2. Are these perceptions different from the perceptions of regular class teaching? 3. Are these perceptions related to sex, age, and educational attainment of the perceivers?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the teaching of special classes is a relatively low prestige occupational area.
special education teaching is perceived as a high prestige occupation in the occupational structure of the United States.
the special class teachers, in the main, do not perceive special education as an occupational area.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
special education teaching is not considered to be a high prestige occupation.
special education teaching is perceived as having a high degree of prestige.
the special class teacher is perceived to carry more prestige than the regular class teacher and that special education as a whole is considered to be a high prestige occupational area.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the special education teaching area is perceived by the general public as having higher prestige than regular teaching, and as having prestige comparable to that of some occupations in the medical field.
special education teaching is perceived by teachers and administrators as being a low prestige occupation.
special education teachers are more likely to be employed in the public sector than in the private sector.
